title: Bash Quick Reference
description: Look up a lesson idea, see its small example, and check a common mistake. Open the linked lesson for setup and practice steps.

entries.name: Print a greeting
entries.summary: printf writes formatted text. %s inserts a string and backslash-n ends the line.
notes: Use a fixed format string so data is not mistaken for formatting.

entries.name: Store a text value
entries.summary: A variable assignment has no spaces around equals. Dollar-name reads the value.
notes: Quote variable expansions so spaces stay inside one value.

entries.name: Add whole numbers
entries.summary: Double parentheses with a dollar sign evaluate integer arithmetic.
notes: Bash arithmetic uses whole numbers, not decimal fractions.

entries.name: Choose a message
entries.summary: [[ ... ]] tests a rule. -ge means greater than or equal for whole numbers.

example.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
score=8
if [[ "$score" -ge 5 ]]; then
 printf 'Pass\n'
else
 printf 'Try again\n'
fi

notes: Use spaces inside [[ and ]] and finish the block with fi.

entries.name: Read an array item
entries.summary: A Bash array keeps indexed values. Its first position is zero.
notes: Braces are needed around an indexed variable expansion.

entries.name: Visit each value
entries.summary: A for loop repeats its body for each word in a list.

example.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
for n in 1 2 3; do
 printf '%s\n' "$n"
done

notes: Use "$@" or quoted array expansion when looping over values with spaces.

entries.name: Name a set of commands
entries.summary: A function groups commands. $1 is its first input.
notes: Function inputs are positional; quote them when reading.

entries.name: Match a label
entries.summary: case chooses commands from text patterns. ;; ends one branch.
notes: End the whole choice with esac.

entries.name: Use a default value
entries.summary: ${name:-Guest} uses Guest when name is unset or empty.
notes: The colon makes an empty value use the fallback too.

entries.name: Count text characters
entries.summary: ${#name} gives the length of the variable value.
notes: For these examples use simple English letters so character counting is clear.

entries.name: Read a command status
entries.summary: A command returns an exit status. Zero usually means success. $? reads the last status.
notes: Read $? immediately; the next command replaces it.

entries.name: Remove a text prefix
entries.summary: The # expansion removes a matching prefix from a value.
notes: This edits the displayed text value; it does not rename a file.
